pl-l3d17c2-d1e114.summary: States that without doubt there were different wills in Christ according to his two natures, the divine will and the human.
claims: Christ had a divine and a human will.

pl-l3d17c2-d1e117.summary: Distinguishes human will as the affection of reason or the affection of sensuality, two different affections of the soul, both called human will. By the affection of reason he willed what the divine will willed, to suffer and die; by the affection of sensuality he did not will it but shrank from it.
claims: Human will is the affection of reason or of sensuality.
By reason Christ willed to die, by sensuality he shrank from death.
concepts: will of reason and of sensuality

pl-l3d17c2-d1e120.summary: Denies that his flesh lusted against the spirit or against God, since, as Augustine says, it is a vice when flesh lusts against spirit. The flesh is said to lust because the soul acts according to it, as it hears through the ear; flesh lusts only through the soul, when the soul with carnal concupiscence resists the spirit, having carnal delight from the flesh against the spirit's delight. The cause of carnal concupiscence lies in neither soul nor flesh alone but in both.
claims: In Christ the flesh did not lust against the spirit.
Flesh lusting against spirit is a vice.
Carnal concupiscence arises from soul and flesh together.

pl-l3d17c2-d1e132.summary: Concludes that no such struggle could be in Christ's soul, since carnal concupiscence could not be there. It was God's will and pleased reason that he will this according to the flesh, to prove the truth of his humanity; who took human nature had to undergo what belongs to it. As in us there is a double affection of mind and sensuality, so in him: by mind to will death, by sensuality not to will it, as in holy men. Peter was led where he did not wish (Jn 21:18), unwilling but overcoming by willing, keeping the natural affection by which no one wishes to die, which even old age did not remove; the Lord said 'let this cup pass', but the force of love conquered. In Christ and his members there is a twofold affection: of reason, formed by charity, willing to die for God; and of sensuality, near the flesh's weakness, shrinking from death.
claims: There was no struggle of concupiscence in Christ.
Christ's sensual shrinking from death proves his true humanity.
Reason formed by charity wills death for God; sensuality shrinks from it.
concepts: will of reason and of sensuality

pl-l3d17c2-d1e151.summary: Cites Augustine: the pious man by the mind's reason desires to be dissolved and be with Christ, but by the sense of the flesh shrinks and refuses; human affection loves life and hates death. By this affection Christ did not will to die, and did not obtain what he asked by it.
claims: By human affection Christ did not will to die and did not obtain what he asked.

pl-l3d17c2-d1e160.summary: Concludes that from the human affection he drew from the Virgin, he willed not to die and prayed that the cup pass.
claims: Christ's human affection willed not to die.

pl-l3d17c2-d1e163.summary: Cites Bede: he prays the cup pass because he is man; here is the human will expressed. See the right heart: 'not what I will but what you will'. Elsewhere: 'I came not to do my will', which I took in time from the Virgin, 'but the will of him who sent me', which I had eternally with the Father. Here two wills in Christ are plainly stated, by which he willed different things.
claims: Christ has a human will from the Virgin and an eternal will with the Father.

pl-l3d17c2-d1e181.summary: Cites Jerome on 'the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak' (Mt 26:41): this is against the Eutychians, who say there is only one will in Christ; it shows the human will, which refuses the passion through the flesh's weakness, and the divine, which is ready to fulfill the dispensation.
claims: Against the Eutychians, Christ has two wills.

pl-l3d17c2-d1e193.summary: Cites Augustine: God's will differs from man's as much as God from man. Bearing man, Christ showed a private human will, figuring his own and ours as our head: 'let this cup pass' was human will, wanting something proper and private. Since he wants man to be upright and directed to God, he adds 'not what I will but what you will', as if to say: see yourself in me, that you can will something of your own while God wills otherwise; this is granted to human frailty.
claims: Christ showed a private human will distinct from God's.
Christ models the submission of our will to God's.

pl-l3d17c2-d1e211.summary: Adds Augustine elsewhere: in the passion Christ expressed two wills according to two natures; 'let this cup pass' is the human will, which he immediately directs to the divine: 'not as I will but as you'.
claims: Christ expressed two wills and directed the human to the divine.

pl-l3d17c2-d1e221.summary: Cites Ambrose, De Trinitate II: 'Father, if possible, take this cup from me' are Christ's words, but spoken as man, bearing man's substance and affection, not as God. He took my will; it is mine that he called his. Yet since all the Father has is his, he has the same will as the Father; Father and Son have one will. But man's will is one thing, God's another: life is in man's will, Christ's passion in the divine will, that he suffer for us.
claims: Christ took a human will.
The Son has one will with the Father.
Human will wanted life; divine will willed the passion.

pl-l3d17c2-d1e258.summary: Concludes that these testimonies plainly teach two wills in Christ; Archbishop Macarius, who denied it, was condemned in a synod.
claims: Christ has two wills.
Macarius was condemned for denying it.

pl-l3d17c2-d1e261.summary: Explains that by human affection of sensuality, not of reason, he willed and asked what he did not obtain. He did not ask in order to obtain it, knowing God would not do it, nor did he will it by reason or divine will. He asked to give his members a pattern: in coming trouble, to cry to the Lord and submit their will to God's, praying for relief when grieved but, if they cannot avoid it, saying what Christ said. So it was not foolish that he was not heard for bodily safety: he asked a good thing, not to die, but it was better that he die, and that happened.
claims: Christ asked by sensuality what he did not obtain.
Christ's prayer gives his members an example of submitting their will.
It was better that Christ die.

pl-l3d17c2.summary: Teaches that Christ had two wills according to his two natures, divine and human. Human will is either the affection of reason or of sensuality: by reason he willed to suffer and die, as the divine will did; by sensuality he shrank from it. This was no conflict of flesh against spirit, since there was no carnal concupiscence in him; it was fitting for the truth of his humanity, as in Peter, led where he did not wish but overcoming his reluctance by love. Bede, Jerome (against the Eutychians), Augustine, and Ambrose confirm two wills; Macarius was condemned for denying it. By the affection of sensuality he asked for what he did not obtain, knowing it would not happen, to give his members an example of praying and submitting their will to God's; he asked a good thing, but it was better that he die.
claims: Christ had two wills, divine and human.
Human will includes the affection of reason and of sensuality.
By reason Christ willed to die; by sensuality he shrank from death.
There was no conflict of flesh against spirit in Christ.
Christ prayed for what he did not obtain to give an example to his members.
concepts: will of reason and of sensuality
